best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-ii.pattern: State-machine DP (holding / not holding), which collapses to a greedy sum of rises

approaches.name: Recursion over each day's choice
approaches.idea: On each day we either do nothing, or act: buy if we hold nothing, sell if we hold a share. Try both and take the best.
steps: `best(i, holding)`: 0 once `i == n`.
Skip: `best(i + 1, holding)`.
Act: if holding, `prices[i] + best(i + 1, false)`; otherwise `−prices[i] + best(i + 1, true)`. Return the larger.
approaches.why: Two branches per day without caching. A share still held at the end adds nothing, so its purchase cost makes that branch lose automatically.

approaches.name: DP table over (day, holding)
approaches.idea: There are only 2n states, so fill them from the last day backwards.
steps: `dp[i][0] = max(dp[i + 1][0], −prices[i] + dp[i + 1][1])` (free: wait or buy).
`dp[i][1] = max(dp[i + 1][1], prices[i] + dp[i + 1][0])` (holding: wait or sell).
Return `dp[0][0]`.
approaches.why: Two states per day, each O(1).

approaches.name: Greedy: collect every rise
approaches.idea: With unlimited transactions, any rising stretch can be split into day-to-day rises, and each rise can be captured by buying the day before and selling that day. So the answer is the sum of all positive day-to-day differences.
steps: For each day `i ≥ 1`, add `max(0, prices[i] − prices[i − 1])`.
Return the total.
approaches.why: One pass. It is exactly the DP above with the two states kept in variables: holding through a rise is the same as selling and re-buying each day.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-with-tra.pattern: State-machine DP with two states: cash (no share) and hold (one share)

approaches.name: Recursion over each day's choice
approaches.idea: Each day, either wait or act (buy when free, sell when holding — paying the fee on the sale). Try both.
steps: `best(i, holding)`: 0 once `i == n`.
Skip: `best(i + 1, holding)`.
Act: if holding, `prices[i] − fee + best(i + 1, false)`; otherwise `−prices[i] + best(i + 1, true)`. Return the larger.
approaches.why: Two branches per day without caching.

approaches.name: DP table over (day, holding)
approaches.idea: Only 2n distinct states — fill them from the last day backwards.
steps: `dp[i][1] = max(dp[i + 1][1], prices[i] − fee + dp[i + 1][0])`.
Return `dp[0][0]`.
approaches.why: Two O(1) states per day.

approaches.name: Two rolling variables
approaches.idea: Walk forward keeping `cash` (best profit with no share) and `hold` (best profit while holding one). Each day, `cash` may sell what `hold` has, and `hold` may buy from `cash`.
steps: Start `cash = 0`, `hold = −prices[0]`.
For each price `p`: `cash = max(cash, hold + p − fee)`; `hold = max(hold, cash − p)`.
Return `cash`.
approaches.why: One pass with two numbers. Using the updated `cash` in `hold` means selling and re-buying on the same day, which only loses the fee, so it never wrongly helps. Profit stays below (n/2)·max price ≈ 1.25·10⁹, inside a 32-bit int.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-iii.pattern: State machine with four states: after first buy, first sell, second buy, second sell

approaches.name: Try every split point
approaches.idea: Two non-overlapping transactions fit on either side of some split day. For every split, find the best single transaction on the left part and on the right part with a scan.
steps: `one(from, to)`: best single transaction in `prices[from..to)` — track the minimum so far and the best `price − min`.
For every split `s` from 0 to n: candidate = `one(0, s) + one(s, n)`.
Return the largest candidate (a split at 0 or n covers using only one transaction).
approaches.why: n + 1 splits, each scanning the whole array.

approaches.name: Prefix best and suffix best arrays
approaches.idea: Precompute the best single transaction ending by each day (left to right) and starting from each day (right to left). Then every split costs O(1).
steps: `left[i]` = best profit within `prices[0..i]`, using a running minimum.
`right[i]` = best profit within `prices[i..n−1]`, using a running maximum from the right; `right[n] = 0`.
Return the maximum of `left[i] + right[i + 1]` over all `i`.
approaches.why: Three linear passes and two arrays.

approaches.name: Four-state machine
approaches.idea: Track the best balance after each stage: first buy, first sell, second buy, second sell. Each stage can only improve from the stage before it on the same day.
steps: Start `buy1 = buy2 = −prices[0]`, `sell1 = sell2 = 0`.
For each price `p`: `buy1 = max(buy1, −p)`; `sell1 = max(sell1, buy1 + p)`; `buy2 = max(buy2, sell1 − p)`; `sell2 = max(sell2, buy2 + p)`.
Return `sell2` (it already covers using one or zero transactions).
approaches.why: One pass, four numbers. Updating in order on the same day only allows buy-and-sell on one day, which adds 0, so it never overcounts.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-iv.pattern: State machine generalised to k transactions: buy[j] and sell[j] per transaction

approaches.name: Recursion over (day, transactions left, holding)
approaches.idea: Each day, wait or act. A transaction is counted when the share is sold; buying is only allowed while some transactions remain.
steps: `best(i, left, holding)`: 0 when `i == n` or `left == 0`.
Skip: `best(i + 1, left, holding)`.
Act: if holding, `prices[i] + best(i + 1, left − 1, false)`; otherwise `−prices[i] + best(i + 1, left, true)`. Return the larger.
approaches.why: Two branches per day without caching.

approaches.name: DP table over (day, transactions left, holding)
approaches.idea: Fill the 2·n·(k + 1) states from the last day backwards.
steps: `dp[n][j][h] = 0`; also `dp[i][0][*] = 0` (no transactions left).
Free: `dp[i][j][0] = max(dp[i + 1][j][0], −prices[i] + dp[i + 1][j][1])`.
Holding: `dp[i][j][1] = max(dp[i + 1][j][1], prices[i] + dp[i + 1][j − 1][0])`.
Return `dp[0][k][0]`.
approaches.why: n·(k + 1)·2 states with O(1) work each.

approaches.name: buy[j] / sell[j] arrays, with the unlimited shortcut
approaches.idea: Generalise the four-state machine from Stock III: `buy[j]` is the best balance holding a share during transaction j, `sell[j]` the best after completing j. If `2k ≥ n`, the limit can never bind, so just sum every rise.
steps: If `2k ≥ n`: return the sum of positive day-to-day differences.
Otherwise start `buy[j] = −prices[0]`, `sell[j] = 0` for j = 1..k (`sell[0] = 0`).
For each price `p`, for j = 1..k: `buy[j] = max(buy[j], sell[j − 1] − p)`; `sell[j] = max(sell[j], buy[j] + p)`.
Return `sell[k]`.
approaches.why: k numbers per day instead of a whole table. A profitable transaction needs at least two days, so at most n/2 can ever be used — which is why the shortcut is exact.

student-attendance-record-ii.pattern: Counting DP over a small state machine: (absences so far, trailing late streak)

approaches.name: Build every eligible record
approaches.idea: Grow the record one day at a time, tracking how many A's it has and how many L's it currently ends with, and count each complete record.
steps: `count(i, a, l)`: 1 when `i == n`.
Add P: `count(i + 1, a, 0)`. Add A if `a == 0`: `count(i + 1, 1, 0)`. Add L if `l < 2`: `count(i + 1, a, l + 1)`.
Sum the branches modulo 10⁹ + 7.
approaches.why: It visits every eligible record one by one, and their number grows exponentially.

approaches.name: DP table over (day, absences, late streak)
approaches.idea: The recursion only depends on `(i, a, l)` — 6 combinations per day. Fill them from the last day backwards.
steps: Return `dp[0][0][0]`.
approaches.why: 6 states per day, O(1) each.

approaches.name: Roll the six states
approaches.idea: Each day only needs the next day's six numbers, so keep two 2 × 3 grids and swap them.
steps: Start `cur[a][l] = 1` for all six states (records of length 0 remaining).
Repeat n times: `next[a][l] = cur[a][0] + (a == 0 ? cur[1][0] : 0) + (l < 2 ? cur[a][l + 1] : 0)` mod 10⁹ + 7; then `cur = next`.
Return `cur[0][0]`.
approaches.why: Six numbers per step. (The transition is a fixed 6 × 6 matrix, so matrix fast power would give O(log n), but O(n) is what interviews expect for n ≤ 10⁵.)

beautiful-arrangement.pattern: Bitmask DP: the set of numbers already used decides the next position

approaches.name: Generate every permutation, then check
approaches.idea: List all n! permutations by swapping, and count those where every position passes the divisibility rule.
steps: Recursively fix each position by swapping every remaining number into it.
At a full permutation, check `perm[i] % i == 0 || i % perm[i] == 0` for every position; count it if all pass.
approaches.why: All n! orders are built, each checked in O(n). n = 15 means 1.3·10¹² permutations — far too many.

approaches.name: Backtracking that only places valid numbers
approaches.idea: Fill positions 1, 2, … in order, and at each position only try unused numbers that already satisfy the rule there. Invalid prefixes are cut off immediately.
steps: `place(pos)`: if `pos > n`, return 1.
For each unused `x` with `x % pos == 0 || pos % x == 0`: mark it used, add `place(pos + 1)`, unmark.
Return the total.
approaches.why: Still exponential in the worst case, but pruning keeps the search to a few hundred thousand calls for n = 15, because most numbers fail at most positions.

approaches.name: Bitmask DP over the set of used numbers
approaches.idea: If `mask` is the set of numbers placed so far, the next position is `popcount(mask) + 1` — the order inside the prefix no longer matters. So count ways per mask.
steps: For each mask in increasing order with `dp[mask] > 0`: `pos = popcount(mask) + 1`.
For each unused number `x` that fits `pos`: `dp[mask | bit(x)] += dp[mask]`.
Return `dp[full]`.
approaches.why: 2ⁿ masks × n candidate numbers — about 5·10⁵ steps for n = 15, regardless of how the pruning would behave.

partition-to-k-equal-sum-subsets.pattern: Bitmask DP: for each set of used numbers, remember how full the current bucket is

approaches.name: Put each number into each bucket
approaches.idea: Try every way of assigning each number to one of k buckets, and accept an assignment where every bucket sums to the target.
steps: Fail fast if the total is not divisible by k; `target = total / k`.
`assign(i)`: at `i == n`, check that every bucket equals `target`.
Otherwise, for each bucket: add `nums[i]`, recurse, take it back.
approaches.why: Each of n numbers has k choices, with no pruning.

approaches.name: Pruned backtracking (largest first)
approaches.idea: Same search, with three cuts: place the largest numbers first, never let a bucket exceed the target, and if a number fails in an empty bucket, it will fail in every other empty bucket too.
steps: Check divisibility and that the largest number ≤ `target`; sort descending.
For `nums[i]`, try each bucket where `bucket + nums[i] ≤ target`.
After trying an empty bucket, stop — the other empty buckets are identical.
Success when every number is placed (each bucket is then exactly `target`).
approaches.why: The same worst case, but the pruning removes symmetric and overfull branches, which in practice cuts the search drastically.

approaches.name: Bitmask DP on the used set
approaches.idea: Fill buckets one after another. Whatever order the numbers in `mask` were placed in, the current bucket holds `sum(mask) % target`. So for each mask just remember whether it is reachable (and that remainder).
steps: Check divisibility; `target = total / k`. `fill[mask] = −1` (unreachable) except `fill[0] = 0`.
For each reachable mask, for each unused `i` with `fill[mask] + nums[i] ≤ target`: `fill[mask | bit(i)] = (fill[mask] + nums[i]) % target`.
Return `fill[full] == 0`.
approaches.why: 2ⁿ masks × n numbers ≈ 10⁶ steps for n = 16. The `≤ target` check means a bucket is never overfilled, so reaching the full mask means every bucket was filled exactly.

minimum-number-of-work-sessions-to-finis.pattern: Bitmask DP storing (sessions used, load of the last session) per set of finished tasks

approaches.name: Backtracking over session assignments
approaches.idea: Take tasks one at a time and put each into any open session with room, or open a new session. Record the fewest sessions over all complete assignments.
steps: `assign(i, used)`: at `i == n`, update the best with `used`.
For each open session `s < used` with `loads[s] + tasks[i] ≤ sessionTime`: add it there and recurse.
Also try opening session `used` with just this task.
approaches.why: It explores every way to group the tasks — the Bell number Bₙ of them (about 1.9·10⁸ for n = 14).

approaches.name: Subset DP: peel off one full session at a time
approaches.idea: `dp[mask]` = fewest sessions to finish the tasks in `mask`. The last session is some sub-mask that fits in one session; the rest is a smaller problem.
steps: Precompute `sum[mask]` for every mask.
`dp[0] = 0`; for each mask, try every non-empty sub-mask `sub` with `sum[sub] ≤ sessionTime`: `dp[mask] = min(dp[mask], dp[mask ^ sub] + 1)`.
Return `dp[full]`.
approaches.why: Enumerating all sub-masks of all masks costs 3ⁿ in total (each task is out, in the rest, or in the session) — about 4.8·10⁶ for n = 14.

approaches.name: Bitmask DP on (sessions, last load)
approaches.idea: Add tasks one at a time. For each set `mask` of finished tasks keep the best pair (sessions used, hours in the last open session), compared first by sessions and then by load. Adding a task either fits in the last session or opens a new one.
steps: `best[0] = (1, 0)` — one empty session open.
For each mask and each unfinished task `t`: if `load + tasks[t] ≤ sessionTime` the pair becomes `(c, load + tasks[t])`, else `(c + 1, tasks[t])`.
Keep the smaller pair for `mask | bit(t)`.
Return the session count of `best[full]`.
approaches.why: 2ⁿ masks × n tasks ≈ 2.3·10⁵ steps for n = 14. Fewer sessions always wins regardless of load, because `(c, anything)` can be turned into `(c + 1, 0)` by opening a fresh session, which beats any `(c + 1, load)`.

shortest-path-visiting-all-nodes.pattern: BFS over (current node, visited set) states — bitmask state-space search

approaches.name: Try every visiting order
approaches.idea: Any walk is described by the order in which nodes are first reached; between two consecutive new nodes, the walk should take a shortest path. So compute all-pairs distances with BFS and try every order.
steps: BFS from every node to get `dist[u][v]`.
For every permutation of the nodes, sum `dist` between consecutive nodes.
Return the smallest sum.
approaches.why: n! orders — fine for a handful of nodes, about 4.8·10⁸ for n = 12.

approaches.name: Multi-source BFS over (node, visited mask)
approaches.idea: A state is "standing at node u having visited set mask". Every edge costs 1, so BFS from all starting states `(i, {i})` at once finds the fewest steps to any state whose mask contains every node.
steps: Push `(i, 1 << i)` for every node with distance 0, marking them seen.
Pop a state; if its mask is full, return its distance.
For each neighbour `v`: the new state is `(v, mask | 1 << v)`; push it if unseen.
approaches.why: n·2ⁿ states, each scanning up to n neighbours. (A Held-Karp DP over `dist` has the same bound; BFS is simpler because edges are unweighted.)

find-the-shortest-superstring.pattern: Held-Karp bitmask DP (travelling-salesman style) on pairwise overlaps

approaches.name: Try every order of the words
approaches.idea: For a fixed order, the shortest string joins each word to the previous one with their largest overlap. Try every order and keep the shortest result.
steps: `overlap(a, b)` = the largest `k` with `a` ending in the first `k` letters of `b` (`k < min(|a|, |b|)`, since no word contains another).
Recursively choose the next unused word, appending `b.substring(overlap(last, b))`.
At a full order, keep the result if it is the shortest so far.
approaches.why: n! orders, each join taking up to O(L²) to find the overlap. Fine for a few words; 12 words would mean 4.8·10⁸ orders.

approaches.name: Held-Karp DP over (used set, last word)
approaches.idea: The result length is `sum of lengths − sum of overlaps between consecutive words`, so maximise total overlap. Like the travelling salesman, the best way to extend an order depends only on which words are used and which came last.
steps: Precompute `ov[i][j]` = overlap of word i followed by word j.
`dp[1 << i][i] = 0`; for every mask, last and unused next: `dp[mask | bit(next)][next] = max(…, dp[mask][last] + ov[last][next])`, remembering `parent`.
Pick the last word with the best `dp[full][last]`; walk `parent` back to recover the order.
Build the answer: the first word, then each next word without its overlapping prefix.
approaches.why: 2ⁿ·n states with n transitions each (≈ 5.9·10⁵ for n = 12), plus the pairwise overlaps of words up to length L.
